name: Plan and execute switching for planned work
summary: Before a crew works on de-energized lines or station equipment, the control room must isolate it with a written switching order and hand the crew a work protection permit. A crew supervisor applies for protection, a switching planner writes the step-by-step order from the network model, a second operator checks it, and on the day a system operator directs field staff by radio through each step before issuing the permit and later restoring the system. Work is slow because orders wait in queues for writing, checking and weekly approval, and because a crew pulled to trouble or bad weather postpones the booked day. Errors are rare but serious: a missed back-feed or wrong device can injure a worker or drop customers.

baseline.org_archetype: A municipally owned Ontario distributor with about 350,000 customers, 91 substations and a 24-hour control room that controls all switching on its system.
baseline.notes: Planned switching only; switching during outages and storms is part of outage restoration. Field switching is done by line crews or station electricians directed by the control room.

trigger: A crew supervisor applies for work protection for a job on the crew schedule.
end_state: The work is done under permit, the system is restored to normal, and the closed order and permit forms are filed; or the work is cancelled.

volume.seasonality: Higher from May to November when most overhead and underground construction is done; lower in deep winter and on hot summer days when load limits restrict transfers.

evidence.note: Organisation file estimate kept: about 60 crews with several isolated jobs a week each. No public count of switching orders was found.

surge.cause: rebuild after a major storm (for example the May 2022 derecho) adds planned switching for permanent repairs

evidence.note: Author's estimate; temporary storm repairs are later rebuilt as planned work under switching orders.
Applies for protection for overhead jobs; underground and station supervisors do the same for theirs. About 25 minutes per order.
Three planners writing about 350 orders a month at the touch times shown; the night-shift operators who check orders do part of the load.
Check, day-of review, direction, permit, restoration and close-out, about 1.1 hours per order across 20 operators on 24-hour shifts.
Weekly approval and occasional revisions.

Two-person field switching, testing, grounding and restoration, about 6 labour hours per order including travel, done by the crews that will do the work; roughly a quarter of the 62 journeypersons' time.
Station switching on about one order in five.

systems.name: Geographic information system (asset and network model)
SCADA for stations and feeder devices
Mobile workforce management and field tablets
Document management and engineering drawing repository

resources.name: Light vehicle (pickup or van) for locators, meter technicians, inspectors and field service

steps.name: Submit application for work protection
steps.description: The crew supervisor fills in the utility's application for work protection for a job on the coming schedule: location, equipment to be isolated, the crew's person in charge, date, start and end times, and whether customers can lose power. A sketch or design print is attached and the form is emailed or entered in the mobile workforce tool.

error.defect_description: Wrong pole or device number, missing isolation point or no customer impact stated.

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Log request and check lead time
steps.description: The switching planner registers the application in the outage management system's planned-work list, checks that it arrived with enough lead time for customer notice, and looks for other orders booked on the same feeder or station that day. Incomplete or late applications go back to the supervisor.

next.condition: returned for missing details or too little notice

evidence.note: Typical controlling-authority intake; return rate is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Study network and load transfer
steps.description: The planner opens the network model in the GIS and OMS and recent feeder loading in SCADA to find the isolation points, decide whether load can be moved to a neighbouring feeder without overloading it, and identify any customers who will lose supply. Abnormal states left by earlier work are checked against the field.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from distribution control-room practice; many orders reuse earlier sequences.

steps.name: Write switching order
steps.description: The planner writes the switching order step by step: each switch or elbow to open, where to apply work permit tags and grounds, the permit to issue, and the reverse restoration steps. Repeat jobs start from a stored order; new ones are written from the single-line diagram.

error.defect_description: Wrong device, missed back-feed path or steps out of order.

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Independently check switching order
steps.description: A second qualified operator, often on a quieter night shift, traces every step of the order against the GIS map and single-line diagram, confirms that all sources into the work zone are opened and grounded, and initials the order. Errors send it back to the planner.

control.basis: Check and recheck of switching orders by a second senior operator before use (controlling-authority practice under the Utility Work Protection Code)

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Approve the week's switching plan
steps.description: The control room shift supervisor reviews all switching orders booked for the coming days in one sitting, looking for conflicts on the same feeders, load limits on hot days, and staffing on each shift. Orders that clash are moved and the planner is told.
inputs: checked switching orders for the week

control.basis: Control centre approval of planned switching before the work day

evidence.note: Weekly review is a common control-centre practice; share with customer interruption is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Send outage details for customer notice
steps.description: For orders that interrupt customers, the planner sends the affected customer list from the OMS, the date, time and expected length to the planned outage notice process so that customers get a call, email or text in advance. The order date is then fixed.

evidence.note: Hydro Ottawa notifies customers of planned outages by phone, email or text; handoff time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review order at start of work day
steps.description: On the booked day the system operator reads the order again, checks SCADA and the OMS for anything that has changed since it was written (a feeder on abnormal, a storm, high load) and confirms by radio that the crew is on site. Work is postponed when the system, weather or crew is not ready.

next.condition: postponed: weather, crew pulled to trouble or system abnormal

evidence.note: Booked lead time follows the customer-notice timeline; postponement and cancellation shares are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Crew confirms readiness and holds job briefing
steps.description: The line crew arrives at the site, holds its tailboard briefing on the hazards and the switching plan, and calls the control room to confirm it is ready, giving the name of the person in charge who will hold the permit.

control.basis: Pre-job tailboard briefing (Electrical Utility Safety Rules)

evidence.note: Pre-job briefing is standard under the Electrical Utility Safety Rules; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Drive to the switching points
steps.description: Two line technicians drive the truck from the work site to each switch, elbow or recloser named in the order, which can be several kilometres apart on rural feeders.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for an urban and rural service area of 1,116 km2.

steps.name: Direct switching step by step
steps.description: The system operator reads each step to the field staff by radio, the field person repeats it back, operates the device and reports the time, and the operator updates the OMS and SCADA model and ticks the step off. Steps that do not match the field stop the sequence.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code (IHSA) permit and tag system used by Ontario distributors with the Electrical Utility Safety Rules

next.condition: field does not match the order

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Stop and revise the sequence
steps.description: When a device is not where the map shows it, is already open or will not operate, the shift supervisor stops the sequence, works out a safe alternative with the operator and approves the revised steps, which are recorded on the order before switching resumes.

error.defect_description: Mismatch left in the GIS model after the revision.

control.basis: Changes to a switching order need control-centre approval before execution

evidence.note: Author's estimate; map and field mismatches are a known source of switching revisions.

steps.name: Operate devices and hang tags
steps.description: The line technicians open the switches or pull the elbows named in each step, check the open point visually, hang work permit tags on every isolating device and report each step back to the operator.

error.defect_description: Wrong device operated or tag missed.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code (IHSA) permit and tag system used by Ontario distributors with the Electrical Utility Safety Rules

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Operate station equipment and hang tags
steps.description: A station electrician opens and racks out the breakers and switches in the substation named in the order, applies work permit tags and locks, and reports each step to the operator by radio or phone.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code (IHSA) permit and tag system used by Ontario distributors with the Electrical Utility Safety Rules

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Test for potential and apply grounds
steps.description: At the work location the crew tests the isolated conductors for voltage and applies protective grounds on both sides of the work zone. The Work Permit protects only the isolation; testing and grounding remain the crew's responsibility.

control.basis: Test for absence of voltage and ground before work (Electrical Utility Safety Rules)

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Issue work protection permit
steps.description: The operator issues the Work Permit by radio to the named person in charge, who writes it down, repeats it back and signs the permit form; the operator records the permit number, holder and time in the OMS and log. Only then may the crew start work.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code (IHSA) permit and tag system used by Ontario distributors with the Electrical Utility Safety Rules

evidence.note: Work Permit issued to a competent person in charge after switching; issuers and holders are certified in the Code. Times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Remove grounds and surrender permit
steps.description: When the planned work is finished the person in charge checks that all workers are clear, the crew removes its grounds, and the holder calls the control room to surrender the permit, which the operator records.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code (IHSA) permit and tag system used by Ontario distributors with the Electrical Utility Safety Rules

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Direct restoration switching
steps.description: The operator cancels the permit and reads the restoration steps in reverse order, removing tags and closing devices, updating the OMS and SCADA model as each step is reported.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code (IHSA) permit and tag system used by Ontario distributors with the Electrical Utility Safety Rules

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Close devices and remove tags
steps.description: The field staff remove the work permit tags and close the devices in the order read by the operator, driving between points as needed, and confirm each step by radio.

evidence.note: Application, check by a second operator, Order to Operate, tags and Work Permit as described for a controlling authority in Ontario; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Confirm customers are back on
steps.description: The operator checks SCADA feeder readings and the OMS for customers still shown off, and checks for calls, before closing the planned outage event. A missed device sends the field staff back.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Close order and update network model
steps.description: The operator enters the actual switching times on the order, sets device states back to normal in the OMS, notes any abnormal state left for the GIS team, and files the order.

error.defect_description: Device state or time not updated.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Review completed orders and file records
steps.description: Once a week the switching planner checks the completed orders and permit forms for missing signatures, times and tags returned, corrects the network model, and files the forms where they are kept for at least two years.

control.basis: Utility Work Protection Code rule 1.101: keep work protection forms and tags at least two years

evidence.note: Two-year retention of work protection forms and tags (UWPC rule 1.101); review effort is the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Order returned at checking
exceptions.description: The second operator finds a wrong device or missed back-feed and returns the order to the planner.

exceptions.name: Postponed on the day
exceptions.description: Weather, a crew pulled to trouble or an abnormal system state postpones the work; the order goes back into the weekly plan and customers may need a second notice.

exceptions.name: Field does not match the order
exceptions.description: A device is missing, already open or will not operate; the shift supervisor approves a revised sequence.

exceptions.name: Station switching
exceptions.description: Isolation is at a substation, so a station electrician on call operates breakers instead of the line crew.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from application for protection to filed order
benchmarks.population: Planned switching orders at a mid-size Ontario distributor, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: applications are usually made one to three weeks before the work so that customers can be notified, and records are filed within a week. No published distribution figure was found.

benchmarks.population: Ontario utilities using the Utility Work Protection Code

evidence.note: Rule 1.101 as reported by IHSA.

pain_points.description: Orders wait for writing, independent checking and the weekly approval, so short-notice jobs cannot be isolated and crews are given other work.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from control-room practice.

pain_points.description: Postponements on the day (weather, trouble calls, abnormal system) waste the crew's set-up and may mean a second customer notice.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: The GIS model does not always match the field, which forces revisions during switching and is a safety risk.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.title: 5.1.5 High Voltage Electrical Systems (Physical Resources safety procedures)
sources.supports: Undated page; year is the access year. An Application for Work Protection goes to the controlling authority (the local hydro utility) ahead of the required date; the utility operator prepares the switching and a second senior operator checks and initials it; the operator switches as written on the Order to Operate, applies work permit tags at every isolating point and issues a Work Permit guaranteeing protection to a competent person; the person in charge on site verifies de-energization, applies grounds and locks out; the holder briefs workers before surrendering the permit.

sources.title: Important concepts for UWPC (IHSA Health and Safety Magazine, volume 23 issue 2)
sources.supports: Undated magazine page; year is the access year. The Utility Work Protection Code works with the Electrical Utility Safety Rules and uses a system of permits and tags to show when lines are isolated and safe to work on; people who issue permits or do the work must be trained and certified in the Code.

sources.title: Electrical utility safety updates (IHSA Health and Safety Magazine, volume 24 issue 1)
sources.supports: Undated magazine page (it says an updated UWPC will be released in 2024); year is the access year. Prepared work protection forms and tags must be kept for at least two years (UWPC rule 1.101); UWPC recertification every 27 months or earlier.

sources.title: Planned power outages
sources.supports: Customers affected by a planned outage receive advance notice by phone, email or text according to their MyAccount preferences, giving date, time and expected length; planned outages are for maintenance, upgrades and crew safety and are kept as short as possible.

assumptions: Loaded costs are taken from the organisation file (wage times 1.40 for benefits, pension, payroll taxes and overhead).
Field switching is done by two line technicians from the crew that will do the work, using its bucket truck; on underground jobs a cable crew does the same steps at similar times.

The time between permit issue and surrender is the planned work itself (another process); it is entered as the wait before the surrender step and is the main reason consoles and trucks are held for hours.
Station switching is done by an on-call station electrician; about one order in five.

lines-supervisor is not listed among this process's roles in the organisation file, but crew supervisors are the usual applicants for work protection; underground-supervisor and stations-supervisor apply in the same way for their jobs.

Three switching planners cannot write 350 orders a month alone at more than an hour each; the night-shift system operators write and check simpler repeat orders, so their share of drafting is counted in the system operator FTE.

Queue waits before the work day are modelled as adding to elapsed time; in practice the work date is booked when the application is made, so these waits are partly absorbed by the booking lead time. The day-of review wait is the remaining time to the booked date. The simulated median (about 15 days) is two days above the 13-day estimate for this reason, and the simulated p90 (about 20 days) is below the estimate because the model does not hold orders booked many weeks ahead for large capital jobs.
